goldenPoints: Goldmann applanation tonometry is the gold standard for IOP.
Acute angle closure: painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, shallow chamber — emergency.
Cherry-red spot at the macula = central retinal artery occlusion.
Leukocoria in a child = retinoblastoma until proved otherwise; Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes.
Bitemporal hemianopia = lesion at the optic chiasma (pituitary tumour).
Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing = occipital (posterior cerebral artery) lesion.
Kayser–Fleischer ring = copper in Descemet membrane = Wilson disease.
Posterior subcapsular cataract = long-term steroid use (also diabetes, radiation).
Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy treats posterior capsular opacification.
Most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults = uveal (choroidal) melanoma.
intro: Ophthalmology carries 15 questions in every FMGE paper and is one of the most image-driven subjects. The stems circle glaucoma emergencies, cataract types and their causes, retinal vascular signs, visual-field localisation, retinoblastoma and classic rings and spots. These 12 topics are built exactly around those repeats.

branches.label: Orbit & nerves
leaves: SOF syndrome = III IV V1 VI

subject: Ophthalmology
tagline: Glaucoma emergencies, cataract causes, retinal signs and visual-field localisation dominate the ophthalmology paper.

topics.askedAs: Painful red eye, oval mid-dilated pupil, shallow chamber
topics.oneLiner: Painful + mid-dilated fixed pupil + shallow chamber + high IOP = acute angle closure — treat as an emergency.
points: Normal IOP is 10–21 mmHg; Goldmann applanation tonometry is the gold standard measurement
Acute angle-closure: sudden severe pain, redness, haloes, nausea; cornea hazy, anterior chamber shallow
Pupil in acute angle closure: fixed, mid-dilated and vertically oval
Primary open-angle glaucoma: painless, progressive peripheral field loss, cupping of the disc
First-line drug class for chronic open-angle glaucoma: prostaglandin analogues (e.g. latanoprost)
Acute attack is broken with IV acetazolamide and hyperosmotics, then pilocarpine once pressure falls
Definitive treatment of angle closure: peripheral iridotomy (laser) — also in the fellow eye
Pilocarpine is contraindicated in secondary glaucomas from inflammation/lens displacement — know the primary angle-closure context
Normal-tension glaucoma: field loss and cupping despite IOP in the normal range
topics.title: Glaucoma: Open-Angle vs Angle-Closure
topics.trap: A mid-dilated pupil in angle closure must NOT be dilated further — and pilocarpine works only after IOP is lowered enough for the iris sphincter to respond.

topics.askedAs: Which cataract in which condition — matching stem
topics.oneLiner: Steroid = posterior subcapsular; galactosaemia = oil drop; trauma = rosette; diabetes = snowflake.
points: Posterior subcapsular cataract: long-term corticosteroids, diabetes, radiation, chronic uveitis
Oil-drop cataract: galactosaemia — early sign, reversible if diet started early
Snowflake cataract: young diabetics; sorbitol accumulation drives diabetic cataract (aldose reductase pathway)
Rosette-shaped cataract: blunt trauma
Sunflower cataract: Wilson disease (copper deposition); chalcosis from a copper foreign body
Second sight: nuclear sclerosis increases lens power — presbyope reads without glasses again
Congenital rubella: cataract + salt-and-pepper retinopathy + PDA and deafness
Most common complication of cataract surgery in follow-up clinics: posterior capsular opacification
PCO is treated by Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy
topics.title: Cataract: Types & Causes
topics.trap: 'Second sight' sounds like improvement — it is worsening nuclear sclerosis and a cataract clue.

topics.askedAs: Sudden painless loss of vision — name the vessel event
topics.oneLiner: CRAO = cherry-red spot + boxcar segmentation; CRVO = blood-and-thunder fundus.
points: Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless monocular blindness, pale retina, cherry-red spot at macula
Cherry-red spot also appears in storage disorders (Tay–Sachs, Niemann–Pick) — context decides
Retinal veins look segmented ('boxcar' / cattle-truck) in CRAO; the eye has roughly 100 minutes before damage is permanent
Amaurosis fugax: transient monocular blindness lasting minutes — emboli from carotid disease
Central retinal vein occlusion: painless loss with widespread flame haemorrhages — 'blood and thunder' fundus
Hypertensive retinopathy (Keith–Wagener grade IV): haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, disc oedema (papilloedema)
Severe NPDR by the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1
Cystoid macular oedema after cataract surgery: petaloid / honeycomb pattern on angiography (Irvine–Gass)
Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters, curtain falling over vision — commoner in myopes
topics.title: Retina: Vascular Occlusions & Diabetic Eye
topics.trap: Flashes + floaters + curtain = detachment (surgical); cherry-red spot = artery occlusion — do not swap them.

topics.askedAs: Field defect shown — localise the lesion
topics.oneLiner: Chiasma cuts the temporal fields; occipital lesions spare the macula.
points: Pituitary tumour compressing the chiasma: bitemporal hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing: occipital lobe / posterior cerebral artery stroke
Homonymous hemianopia with macular splitting: optic radiation or tract lesion
Optic nerve lesion: monocular vision loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)
Retrobulbar neuritis: painful eye movements, RAPD, normal-looking disc, central scotoma
Papillitis: same symptoms but the disc is swollen — the disc appearance separates them
Argyll Robertson pupil: light reflex absent, near reflex present — classically neurosyphilis; lesion in midbrain/pretectal area
Horner syndrome: miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis, pupil stays small in the dark
Superior orbital fissure syndrome: CN III, IV, V1 and VI — ophthalmoplegia with ptosis
topics.title: Neuro-Ophthalmology: Fields, Pupils & Pathways
topics.trap: Macular sparing points BEHIND the radiation to the occipital pole — a favourite localisation trap.

topics.askedAs: Branching / satellite / ring — identify the ulcer
topics.oneLiner: Dendrite = herpes; satellites = fungus; ring infiltrate + lens wear = Acanthamoeba.
points: Corneal transparency is maintained by dermatan sulfate (the key glycosaminoglycan of corneal stroma)
Herpes simplex keratitis: dendritic (branching) ulcer with terminal bulbs; painless relative to its look
Fungal keratitis: vegetative-matter injury, feathery margins, satellite lesions, hypopyon
Aspergillus shows septate hyphae branching at acute angles on microscopy
Acanthamoeba keratitis: contact-lens wearer, severe pain out of proportion, ring infiltrate
Pseudomonas: rapid, grey-white serpiginous ulcer in lens wearers — can melt the cornea
A corneal opacity improves vision with a pinhole when irregular astigmatism is the problem
Descemetocele: deep ulcer with Descemet membrane bulging through — perforation threatens
Trypan blue dye stains the anterior capsule to visualise it during cataract surgery
topics.title: Cornea: Ulcers, Keratitis & Transparency
topics.trap: Steroids worsen herpes and fungal ulcers — stems often hide steroid use in the history.

topics.askedAs: Golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery
topics.oneLiner: KF ring = copper in Descemet membrane = Wilson disease; sunflower cataract keeps it company.
points: Kayser–Fleischer ring: golden to greenish-brown copper ring at the corneal periphery (Descemet membrane)
It signals Wilson disease — check liver enzymes and neurology in the same patient
Hudson–Stahli line, Fleischer ring (keratoconus) and KF ring are three different 'rings' — read the stem
Siderosis bulbi: iron foreign body deposits iron — rusty discoloration, cataract, retinal damage
Chalcosis: copper foreign body — sunflower cataract and KF-like ring
HLA association asked with eye stems: HLA-B27 with acute anterior uveitis
Koeppe nodules sit at the pupillary margin of the iris in granulomatous uveitis (sarcoidosis)
CMV retinitis in AIDS: ganciclovir is the drug of choice; fundus looks like 'pizza pie' / ketchup-and-cheese
Shield ulcer is seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis (spring catarrh)
topics.title: Rings, Deposits & Uveitis Clues
topics.trap: Fleischer ring belongs to keratoconus; Kayser–Fleischer belongs to Wilson — the examiners count on the shared surname.

topics.askedAs: Child with white reflex / rosettes on histology
topics.oneLiner: Leukocoria + Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes = retinoblastoma — never biopsy an intraocular tumour.
points: Retinoblastoma: commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood; leukocoria and strabismus are the presenting signs
Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathology confirm retinoblastoma
Gene: RB1 on chromosome 13q14; bilateral cases are heritable
Most common primary intraocular malignancy in ADULTS: uveal (choroidal) melanoma
Amblyopia: reduced vision with a normal-looking eye; commonest cause is strabismus / unequal refraction
Anisometropia: different refractive power in the two eyes — a silent amblyopia cause
Amblyopia treatment: correct refraction and PATCH the good (normal) eye; atropine penalisation is an alternative
Accommodative esotropia: full hypermetropic correction with glasses is the main treatment
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking: lid rises when the child sucks/chews — trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis
topics.title: Paediatric Eye: Leukocoria, Amblyopia & Squint
topics.trap: Patch the GOOD eye in amblyopia — patching the lazy eye is the classic reversed answer.

topics.askedAs: Bitot spot / xerosis grade in a malnourished child
topics.oneLiner: Bitot spots = X1B; xerophthalmia is a public-health problem above 0.5% Bitot prevalence.
points: Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia: night blindness is the earliest symptom
Conjunctival xerosis and Bitot spots (foamy, triangular, at the limbus) follow night blindness
WHO grade X1B = Bitot spots; corneal xerosis/ulceration come later and scar
Xerophthalmia is a public-health problem if Bitot spot prevalence exceeds 0.5% in children
Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis: seasonal itching, ropy discharge, Horner–Trantas dots, shield ulcer — mast-cell mediated
Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis: yellowish nodules at the limbus in undernourished children — hypersensitivity to tubercular/staphylococcal antigen
Pterygium: fleshy growth from conjunctiva onto cornea; recurrent pterygium is managed with excision + conjunctival autograft
Normal conjunctival flora most commonly includes Staphylococcus epidermidis
topics.title: Vitamin A, Conjunctiva & Community Eye Health
topics.trap: Night blindness precedes Bitot spots — 'earliest' and 'most common sign asked' are different answers.

topics.askedAs: Swelling at inner canthus / pus point at a lash
topics.oneLiner: Dacryocystitis → DCR; stye = Zeis; chalazion = meibomian; recurrent chalazion — rule out sebaceous carcinoma.
points: Chronic dacryocystitis: watering, discharge, swelling at the medial canthus; treatment of choice is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)
External DCR removes lacrimal and frontal-process-of-maxilla bone to open the sac into the nose
Stye (hordeolum externum): painful pus point at a lash base — gland of Zeis (or Moll)
Chalazion: painless, firm, away from the lid margin — meibomian gland lipogranuloma
Multiple recurrent chalazia: suspect sebaceous gland carcinoma of the lid
Lagophthalmos (inability to close the eye) follows facial nerve (CN VII) palsy
Angular dermoid cyst sits at the external angular (frontozygomatic) region — excise completely
Proptosis that increases on bending forwards / Valsalva: orbital varix (venous malformation)
Dry eye with poor Schirmer test despite normal acuity explains reading strain in stems
topics.title: Lids, Lacrimal System & Orbit
topics.trap: Stye is Zeis; chalazion is meibomian — stems describe both as 'lid swelling' and expect the gland.

topics.askedAs: Down-and-out eye / diplopia on stairs / evening ptosis
topics.oneLiner: Down-and-out + dilated pupil = CN III; stairs + head tilt = CN IV; evening ptosis = myasthenia.
points: CN III palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, pupil dilated (surgical/third-nerve) — diabetes usually spares the pupil
CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia worst on descending stairs/reading; head tilts away from the lesion
CN VI palsy: horizontal diplopia, eye cannot abduct; common in raised intracranial pressure (false localising sign)
Yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus is the left medial rectus
Levo-depression is produced by left inferior rectus + right superior oblique
Myasthenia gravis: ptosis and diplopia worsening with exertion and towards evening; edrophonium (Tensilon) test improves it
Cover–uncover test detects tropias (manifest squint) — it cannot detect refractive error / field defects
Superior oblique is supplied by CN IV, lateral rectus by CN VI, all others by CN III (LR6 SO4 rule)
Total ophthalmoplegia localises to the cavernous sinus / orbital apex region
topics.title: Extraocular Muscles & Cranial Nerve Palsies
topics.trap: Pupil involvement in CN III palsy points to compression (aneurysm); pupil sparing points to diabetes.

topics.oneLiner: Deep chamber + black pupil + +12 D glasses = aphakia; myopia takes a concave lens.
points: Aphakia: deep anterior chamber, jet-black pupil, iridodonesis; corrected with about +10 to +12 D spectacles
Myopia: concave (minus) lenses; child holds books close and squints at the board
Hypermetropia: convex (plus) lenses; can cause accommodative esotropia in children
Astigmatism: rays focus at different points in different meridians — cylindrical lens corrects it
Posterior staphyloma on indirect ophthalmoscopy = pathological (degenerative) myopia
Indirect ophthalmoscopy gives an inverted, magnified image with a wide field — good for the periphery
High myopes are prone to retinal detachment — deep anterior chamber with flashes/floaters is the stem
Blindness category: vision worse than 3/60 but better than 1/60 in the better eye (with field <10°) is classified as blindness per Indian/WHO-based definitions used in stems
Pinhole improves vision in refractive error and irregular corneal astigmatism, not in retinal disease
topics.title: Refractive Errors & Aphakia
topics.trap: Aphakia needs a strong PLUS lens; pseudophakia means an IOL is in place — opposite stem pictures.

topics.oneLiner: No fundus glow + painless sudden loss = vitreous haemorrhage; hand-movement vision + endophthalmitis = vitrectomy pathway.
points: Sudden painless vision loss with absent fundus glow and no trauma: vitreous haemorrhage (diabetes, Eales disease)
Post-cataract endophthalmitis with vision of hand movements only: needs vitreous tap/intravitreal antibiotics ± vitrectomy per EVS logic
Curtain-falling sign is the classic description of retinal detachment
CRAO causes sudden painless loss; painful sudden loss with RAPD and normal disc = retrobulbar neuritis
Siderosis from an iron foreign body changes colour vision early and damages the retina
Trypan blue is the dye used to stain the anterior capsule in cataract surgery
IOL power in infants under 1 year accounts for the eye's future growth — deliberate under-correction is planned
Congenital glaucoma: photophobia, watering, large clear cornea (buphthalmos) with Haab striae
Haab striae are breaks in Descemet membrane from corneal stretching in congenital glaucoma
topics.title: Sudden Vision Loss & Surgical Emergencies
topics.trap: Haab striae = congenital glaucoma; they are horizontal/curved Descemet breaks, not corneal ulcers.
